items.title: POSIX wordexp(3) is dangerous
items.content:
wordexp(3) is a POSIX API for performing shell-style expansions from C.

It's often cited/recommended as a way to do tilde expansion (e.g. ~/foo to /home/me/foo ):

However, wordexp(3) is also dangerous! That last 0 argument is for the flags parameter.

By default, all expansion features are enabled, including command expansion :

Disabling this requires passing WRDE_NOCMD as a flag. Unfortunately, this

palliative at best in some libc implementations:

musl implements wordexp(3) by delegating to the system shell. It adds some

perfunctory scanning for command substitutions before delegating, but

fails to match some patterns that the underlying shell (like GNU Bash) can treat

macOS's libc implements wordexp(3) in a similar manner, delegating to

/usr/lib/system/wordexp-helper 1 . According to Julian Squires

this had the same bypass as musl as recently as 2023 , although I didn't bother

testing whether it's still effective now that the default macOS shell is zsh

Bottom line: don't use wordexp(3) on untrusted inputs, even with WRDE_NOCMD .

Previously, macOS's wordexp(3) would shell out to Perl. wordexp-helper appears to be the "modern" solution. ↩
items.title_ko: POSIX wordexp(3)은 위험하다
items.summary_ko: wordexp(3)은 쉘 방식의 확장을 C에서 수행하는 POSIX API로, 틸드 확장 용도로 자주 추천된다. 그러나 기본적으로 명령 치환까지 활성화되어 있어 신뢰할 수 없는 입력에 쓰면 위험하다. WRDE_NOCMD 플래그도 musl과 macOS libc 등 일부 구현에서는 충분한 방어가 되지 않는다.
items.content_ko: wordexp(3)은 C에서 쉘 스타일 확장을 수행하는 POSIX API이며, `~/foo`를 `/home/me/foo`로 바꾸는 틸드 확장 용도로 자주 권장된다. 하지만 기본 설정에서는 명령 치환을 포함한 모든 확장 기능이 켜져 있어 위험하다. 이를 막으려면 WRDE_NOCMD 플래그를 넘겨야 한다. 그러나 musl은 wordexp를 시스템 쉘에 위임하면서 명령 치환을 일부만 검사하기 때문에, GNU Bash가 처리할 수 있는 일부 패턴을 놓친다. macOS libc도 `/usr/lib/system/wordexp-helper`에 위임하는 방식이며, 작성자는 Julian Squires의 설명을 인용해 2023년까지 musl과 같은 우회 방법이 통했다고 전했다. 작성자의 결론은 WRDE_NOCMD를 쓰더라도 신뢰할 수 없는 입력에는 wordexp(3)을 사용하지 말라는 것이다.

items.title: ChatGPT Is Building Detailed Psychological Profiles of Its Users:  system is acting as your advisor, your friend, your doctor, your lawyer, and so it has information on everything.
items.content:
Chatbots are building intimate “algorithmic self-portraits” of users as they retain information to offer a hyper-personalized experience, researchers warn.

A recent study , conducted by a coalition of scientists in Germany, India and the Netherlands and presented at the ACM Web Conference 2026, investigated the ways that OpenAI’s ChatGPT has tracked and made sense of user inputs to develop comprehensive digital profiles of users.

In an already-personalized era of digital life defined by data-powered recommendation algorithms, the study urges that chatbot memory offers a “new form of personalization derived from users’ self-disclosed information divulged within private conversations,” a reality that poses privacy risks and which the researchers believe demands “closer examination of the underlying mechanisms that enable such personalization.”

Drawing on the donated chat logs of 80 real-world ChatGPT users who obtained their conversation history by way of European data privacy laws, the researchers were able to identify 2,050 memory entries across the AI interactions of 65 users.

A staggering 96 percent of memories were created unilaterally by the chatbot, according to the study, meaning that the users had little overt control over the data points that ChatGPT logged as their interactions wore on. Stored memories were also deeply revealing about users. About 28 percent of the memories examined contained personal data as defined by Europe’s strict General Data Protection Regulation standards, and 52 percent contained rich “psychological insights” about users.

“Earlier, the platforms had one objective: to sell you ads and to mediate an interaction between you and an advertiser,” lead author Abhisek Dash told Gizmodo . “But now, they are actually talking to you, so they may want to know more about you so that they can have an effective conversation.”

At times, the researchers found, the memories that ChatGPT was logging were sometimes based on presumptions. For example, when one user asked the chatbot to “give me bands like Nirvana,” ChatGPT noted that the user “likes Nirvana” — a determination that, as the study notes, “is not explicitly stated and relies on an assumption.” (Per the study, ChatGPT did annotate this assumption as “weakly supported.”)

The study does have limits, the chief being that, as Gizmodo notes, OpenAI’s memory system has been updated. (In January, OpenAI introduced what it called a “more capable and scalable system for synthesizing memory.”) Users may also opt out of stored memory features.

Memory has utility. Frequent AI users might not want to constantly remind a chatbot what they do for work when they’re trying to send emails, for example. But it can also be a powerful driver of engagement, and sometimes for the worst : as Futurism has reported , a major ChatGPT memory upgrade back in April 2025 was closely tied to many instances of “AI psychosis,” or cases in which people enter into delusional spirals with ChatGPT and other bots .

According to Dash, chatbots’ role as a relational technology raises novel privacy risks, too. After all, many users may not be engaging with chatbots as if they’re tools, and might instead be treating them like a coworker or even as a friend — and we tell our friends some very personal details.

“That is the privacy risk which is sort of emerging, because there is no boundary anymore; the system is acting as your advisor, your friend, your doctor, your lawyer, and so it has information on everything,” Dash told Gizmodo . “If the system knows you so well, and if its objective is to cater to your beliefs and validate your thoughts sycophantically to have you come back to it time and again, then it can have disastrous broader implications, anywhere from extreme political polarization to reinforcement of prejudices and biases.”

More on AI and memory: New Paper Proposes What Really Causes AI Psychosis
items.title_ko: ChatGPT가 사용자의 심리 프로필을 상세하게 구축하고 있다는 연구
items.summary_ko: 독일, 인도, 네덜란드 연구진이 ChatGPT의 메모리 기능이 사용자 대화를 바탕으로 개인 프로필을 만든다는 연구를 발표했다. 연구진은 80명의 실제 사용자 대화 기록을 분석해 65명에게서 2,050개의 메모리 항목을 찾았다. 전체 메모리의 96%는 사용자가 아니라 챗봇이 자체적으로 생성한 것으로 나타났다.
items.content_ko: 연구진은 챗봇이 사용자에 대해 보유한 정보를 바탕으로 맞춤형 경험을 제공하면서 친밀한 '알고리즘 자화상'을 만들고 있다고 경고했다. 이 연구는 ACM Web Conference 2026에서 발표되었으며, 독일, 인도, 네덜란드 과학자들이 함께 수행했다. 연구진은 유럽 개인정보 보호법을 통해 대화 기록을 받은 80명의 실제 ChatGPT 사용자 데이터를 분석했다. 그 결과 65명의 AI 대화에서 2,050개의 메모리 항목을 확인했다. 연구에 따르면 메모리의 96%는 챗봇이 일방적으로 생성한 것이다. 연구진은 이것이 사용자가 사적인 대화에서 스스로 밝힌 정보에서 비롯된 새로운 형태의 개인화이며, 프라이버시 위험을 안고 있어 기반 메커니즘에 대한 더 면밀한 검토가 필요하다고 주장했다. 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
items.content:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust ) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying

[W]e should be more ambitious 1 with the software we build

There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail , this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath , this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail , multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader 2 , this money overflow bug , etc.

This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free 3 , but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.

That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).

As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday , and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.

But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.

If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.

Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:

At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about , this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun"…
items.title_ko: 우리는 우리가 만드는 소프트웨어에 더 야심을 가져야 한다
items.summary_ko: 글쓴이는 pgrust 프로젝트를 만든 Michael Malis의 작업을 근거로, 소프트웨어에 더 큰 야심을 가져야 한다고 주장한다. AI로 만든 저품질 프로젝트가 많아 pgrust에도 회의적인 시선이 있지만, Malis는 pgrust를 테스트하는 과정에서 Postgres의 실제 버그들을 여럿 찾아냈다. pgrust가 완벽하지는 않더라도, 시도 자체가 Postgres를 개선하는 데 기여했다고 평가한다.
items.content_ko: 글쓴이는 올해 초부터 Michael Malis가 보여준 여러 작업물을 보며, 소프트웨어는 더 야심 있게 만들어야 한다고 말해 왔다. pgrust 같은 프로젝트에는 저품질 AI 생성 프로젝트가 많다는 이유로 회의적인 시선이 있다. 하지만 글쓴이는 Malis를 신뢰하며, 직접 살펴보면 그가 pgrust를 충분히 철저하게 테스트하고 있다고 말한다. 그 과정에서 Postgres의 실제 버그가 여럿 드러났다. 예를 들어 유효한 SP-GiST 연산이 실패하게 만드는 수치 버그, JSONPath에서 잘못된 결과를 내게 하는 format cache 버그, 이후 연산을 실패하게 만드는 pgcrypto 버그, 사전 로더의 여러 메모리 안전성 버그, 금액 오버플로 버그 등이다. 글쓴이는 pgrust가 버그가 없다는 뜻은 아니라고 덧붙인다. 하지만 상당한 양의 테스트가 이루어지고 있으며, pgrust가 끝내 성공하지 못하더라도 이런 시도 자체가 Postgres를 여러 면에서 개선했다고 주장한다.

items.title: The Slurptop: A home-built luggable that runs on power tool batteries
items.content:
Table of Contents The Design Process | Power Delivery | Bill of Materials | Closing Thoughts

Prior to completing this project I didn't have a modern laptop. I also had never tried out a trackball mouse. After completing a Writerdeck and a Cyberdeck based on Raspberry Pi SBCs, I felt that it would be incredibly useful to have a full-fledged x86 portable computer. You know, a laptop. Why not spend two months designing, building, and refining a laptop myself instead of just hitting up Best Buy for a new laptop that's ready to go? I mean, I don't have good justification beyond "because I can, and I want to", but sometimes that's all the justification you need!

At the outset of the design process I started looking at Intel N50 and N100 mITX motherboards and PicoPSU power delivery, but started getting discouraged at the price prospect of something that was more expensive than a Raspberry Pi, consumed more power, didn't offer much more computing power than a Pi, and consumed significantly more power. That's when I figured if I was heading in a high power draw x86 setup, why not start shopping out some mini PCs?

That's where I found some decently spec'd out units with laptop processors and integrated graphics. These, I figured, would fit the bill for a machine that would be destined for some coding and light design work. Next up would be figuring out the power delivery.

Since my last folding screen Cyberdeck, I've been really enjoying designing within the Cyberpunk aesthetic. One of the aesthetic aspects that I felt the last build was missing was improvised part selection. Then I had the thought of powering the unit with a 24v power tool battery. The design aesthetic and the improvised hardware selection dovetailed beautifully in the design of the power delivery. The mini PC I bought had a 19v/5a power supply, and my power tool batteries were 24v. With a properly spec'd boost/buck converter, that should work perfectly both on the aesthetic requirement as well as the power and current requirement.

Now we get to the fun stuff: sketching out the design.

If you're interested in Cyberdecks, I'm sure you've seen a plethora of devices. From slabs without a hinging screen, to vintage computer style raising screens (like I used on my gray Cyberdeck), to absolutely awesome sliding designs like u/Personalitysphere's sliding modular Cyberdeck. I wanted something that would have the rough form factor of a laptop.

With the form factor decided on, the next step in every project I do is to gather up all the components, grab my calipers, and get to measuring and modeling in Blender. I make "good enough" 3d models of EVERYTHING. It's tedious and time consuming, but I wouldn't do it any other way. You can package everything so much nicer when using this method, and you run into WAY fewer problems during the assembly stage, WAY fewer redesigns and reprints, etc. This is the "measure twice" process when building a device like this, even though it's more along the lines of "measuer ten thousand times". Very worth it, and I highly recommend approaching things from this direction. Not to mention you're honing your ability to measure and model things, which is invaluable as a desinger.

After establishing the layout of the individual components, I start going through a process of sketching out designs and layouts. Usually I have a pretty clear vision of what I'm going for at this point, but a lot of design elements are "discovered" at this stage. It's also where some hard choices have to be made because establishing certain design elements sets you down a road where if you choose to go a different direction you can't just CTRL+Z you're way out of. You have to delete a LOT of work sometimes.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Retro Gaming Has a Port-Slop Problem
items.content:
One thing I’ve always loved the homebrew scene, particularly when it involves old hardware, is when someone decides that a console or handheld should be capable of doing something it was never designed for, spends an unreasonable amount of time figuring out how to make it happen, and eventually emerges with a working piece of software that nobody would have thought possible. Sometimes it's a remarkably faithful port of a game, sometimes an entirely new emulator, and occasionally it's something so thoroughly impractical that you have to admire the effort involved.

Lately, though, I've noticed a change in the kinds of projects being shared across retro gaming communities. Games are apparently being ported to everything , and at a pace that would have seemed completely ridiculous even a year ago. Titles that once would have represented months or years of work are being announced in a matter of days (or multiple times each day), often accompanied by an exciting screenshot, a short demonstration and a GitHub repository. At first, I thought this was wonderful. More homebrew, more interest in old hardware, and more people experimenting with games that have long since been abandoned by their original publishers. What's not to like?

Well, quite a bit, as it turns out. Because somewhere in this sudden explosion of activity, I think we've started confusing getting a game to run with actually creating a worthwhile port.

There's a term being thrown around increasingly often now: port-slop . It's not a particularly pleasant phrase, but I can understand why it's caught on. It describes the growing collection of AI-assisted ports, recompilations and other projects which appear with great fanfare, demonstrate just enough functionality to attract attention, and then seemingly move on anybody has established whether they're actually enjoyable to play. Not every project deserves that description, of course, and there are people doing impressive things with these tools. But there's enough questionable work appearing that it's becoming difficult to separate a promising development effort from something produced primarily because an AI model made it possible to produce. So naturally I think that's a problem worth talking about.

Getting it running is only the beginning

AI coding tools such as Claude have changed what's possible for hobbyist developers. There's little point pretending otherwise. Tasks that once demanded substantial programming knowledge can now be approached by people who might never have written software themselves, while experienced developers can use those same tools to accelerate repetitive work, investigate problems and experiment with solutions that would otherwise take much longer to develop. I find that genuinely exciting, particularly when it comes to old consoles whose limitations have discouraged projects for years, but I also think we've become a little too impressed by the earliest stage of the process.

Getting a game to boot is an achievement, especially on hardware that was never intended to run it. It's also often the easiest part to demonstrate. A title screen makes for a fantastic screenshot, and a few seconds of recognizable gameplay can be enough to send an announcement racing around social media. What those demonstrations rarely tell us is whether the rest of the game works, whether performance remains acceptable after the opening area, whether saving is reliable, or whether the controls have been properly adapted to the target hardware. They don't tell us whether anybody has played the thing for several hours, let alone finished it.

Consider the PSP. Sony's handheld is an extraordinary little machine which is my personal favorite, but it isn't exactly swimming in resources by modern standards. The original PSP-1000 has just 32MB of RAM, with later models doubling that to 64MB, and of course the system has that single analogue slider. items.title: Day 16 - Archiving and compressing
items.content:
As a system administrator, you need to be able to confidently work with compressed “archives” of files. In particular two of your key responsibilities; installing new software, and managing backups, often require this.

On other operating systems, applications like WinZip, and pkzip before it, have long been used to gather a series of files and folders into one compressed file - with a .zip extension.

Archiving and compressing, however, are actually distinct processes that are frequently used together. Archiving consolidates multiple files into one “box” while preserving their structure and attributes, but it does not change the total data size. Compression uses sophisticated algorithms to encode data efficiently, saving storage space by shrinking that file.

The goal of compression is to reduce file size. Smaller files use less bandwidth and can be transmitted over networks faster. Different tools use different algorithms to actually shrink that data.

Note 1: The -f switch specifies that “the output should go to the filename which follows” - so in this case the order of the switches is important. VERY IMPORTANT : tar considers anything after -f as the name of the archive that needs to be created. So, we should always use -f as the last flag while creating an archive.

Note 2: The -v switch (verbose) is included to give some feedback - traditionally many utilities provide no feedback unless they fail.

(The cryptic “tar” name? - originally short for “tape archive”)

You could then compress this file with GnuZip like this:

…which will create myinits.tar.gz . A compressed tar archive like this is known as a “tarball”. You will also sometimes see tarballs with a .tgz extension - at the Linux commandline this doesn’t have any meaning to the system, but is simply helpful to humans.

In practice you can do the two steps in one with the -z switch, like this:

This uses the -c switch to say that we’re creating an archive; -v to make the command “verbose”; -z to compress the result - and -f to specify the output file.

To “explode” an archive and retrieve your files, use the -x (extract) flag:

Safety First: Before extracting, it is a good practice to preview the contents using the -t (list) flag:

That gives you an idea of how the file structure will look like after extracting. If the list shows many files without a common prefix (like folder/file), you have found a tarbomb . No, not this one . Extracting this may spew files directly into your current directory, potentially overwriting existing files.

You can use the -C flag to extract files into a specified target directory to keep things tidy.

You might notice that some tutorials write tar cvf rather than tar -cvf with the switch character - do you know why? Hint : It’s related to old “tape archive” styles and modern compatibility.

Level 1: Fast, but provides low compression.

Level 6: The default setting; a balance of speed and size.

items.summary_ko: 시스템 관리자에게 아카이빙과 압축은 소프트웨어 설치와 백업에 필요한 핵심 작업이다. 아카이빙은 여러 파일을 구조와 속성을 유지한 채 하나로 묶는 것이며, 데이터 크기를 줄이지는 않는다. 압축은 알고리즘으로 데이터를 줄여 저장 공간과 전송 시간을 아끼는 것이다. 본문은 GZip으로 압축하는 예시를 소개한다.
items.content_ko: 시스템 관리자는 압축된 아카이브 파일을 능숙하게 다룰 수 있어야 하며, 이는 소프트웨어 설치와 백업 관리에 특히 필요하다. 다른 운영체제에서 WinZip이나 pkzip이 여러 파일과 폴더를 하나의 압축 파일로 묶는 데 쓰여 온 것처럼 말이다. 아카이빙과 압축은 서로 다른 과정이지만 함께 쓰이는 경우가 많다. 아카이빙은 파일의 구조와 속성을 유지하면서 여러 파일을 하나의 '상자'에 모으는 것이며, 전체 데이터 크기는 바뀌지 않는다. 압축은 정교한 알고리즘으로 데이터를 효율적으로 인코딩해 파일을 줄이고 저장 공간을 아낀다. 압축의 목적은 파일 크기를 줄이는 것이며, 작은 파일은 대역폭을 덜 쓰고 네트워크로 더 빨리 전송된다. 본문은 GZip으로 파일을 압축하는 명령 예시를 보여준다. 이 명령은 my-big-file.gz를 만들지만 원본 파일을 대체한다는 점을 설명하며 끝난다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-115635 📢 Source: EEF 💣 CVSS Score: 6 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash_postgres allows a user to read another tenant's record through a skipped upsert. When Ash.bulk_create/4 or a single create runs as an upsert with return_skipped_upsert?: true and the upsert is skipped (for example because its upsert_condition does not hold), AshPostgres.DataLayer reads the existing row back by the upsert identity in do_bulk_create/3 and upsert/4. That lookup did not apply the resource's attribute multitenancy, so on a resource using strategy :attribute it could match and return the row of another tenant with the same identity values, exposing its fields to the caller. This issue affects ash_postgres: from 2.6.22 before 2.15.2. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-25T19:48:43.829Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115635

items.title: The Goose Programming Language
items.content:
A memory-safe systems language with no heap allocator, garbage

collector, or lifetime annotations. In this repository's benchmarks,

Goose runs faster than C++ and Rust while using less memory.

Tutorial · Reference · Specification · Packages · Samples · Benchmarks · Standard library

Goose has syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, but

there is no heap . Every dynamic value lives inline on a

data stack managed by the compiler. Growth advances a pointer, and

memory is freed when its scope ends. The language's type and lifetime

rules make this memory model safe to use.

the whole language topic by topic, the specification has the exact rules, and

This section focuses on what distinguishes Goose. The tutorial explains these features in more

A program has the native call stack, static data and N data stacks,

where the compiler works out N. A data stack is a large address-space

reservation with a bump pointer, and there is no other memory. At most

one resizable value is live per stack and it is always on top, so growth

never moves anything and never checks a capacity. All of this is proved

at compile time; the runtime tracks only the bump pointers.

push returns a reference to the new element, so a

program can link elements while building the array. A

and cannot provide this guarantee. Stable references account for several

Every reference and slice has a static root : the variable

that bounds its target's lifetime. A reference must not outlive the

variable that owns its target or access that target through an

incompatible type. The compiler infers roots and specializes functions

for them, so no annotations are needed. There are no aliasing or

exclusivity rules. When a lifetime check fails, the error names the

A slice T[:] lets a function accept a range from any

array kind without copying its elements. For example, split

returns slices into its input, and a dictionary keyed by

u8[:] stores views of strings rather than copies.

There is no single array type. There is a family that differs only in

what happens to the size, and every member is

[metadata][elements...] , inline and packed, never a pointer

Strings are just u8 arrays: u8[>..] is a

builder, u8[] a finished string stored inline in whatever

holds it, u8[..16] a small string inside a struct,

u8[:] a view. A struct may contain variable-size parts, and

they sit inline in declaration order, so a record is a run of bytes with

That order is 29 bytes and 0 allocations . As C++

160 bytes and 1 allocation, and as Rust String +

Vec<Item> 153 bytes and 4. A whole order book is one

array that streams through the cache. The price is that an array of

variable-size elements is sequential: you can iterate it but not index

it (unless you keep a second array of references into it as an

Algebraic data types are the only dynamic polymorphism: no

inheritance, no vtables. Every ADT can be stored two ways, chosen at the

point of use. Fixed mode ( Shape ) is a tag plus room for the

largest payload, indexable and overwritable. Variable mode

( Shape.. ) gives each value exactly its variant's size; the

array becomes sequential and a value never changes variant, and in

exchange you may take references into a payload:

Case functions provide another way to dispatch on a variant:

define one overload per variant. Calls dispatch on the tag through a

jump table, and the compiler checks that the overloads cover every

A T& is a machine address: eight bytes, never

dangling. A relative reference is the same link stored as a

narrow offset: T&<u32> is measured from the field

itself to a target in the same array, so the structure is position

independent, and T&<u32 in pool> from a named

pool's base, so other arrays can link into the pool.

T&<u32>? uses offset 0 as null. Here is a binary

items.title_ko: Goose 프로그래밍 언어
items.summary_ko: Goose는 힙 할당기, 가비지 컬렉터, 수명 주석이 없는 메모리 안전 시스템 언어다. 저장소의 벤치마크 기준으로 C++와 Rust보다 빠르면서도 메모리를 적게 쓴다고 소개된다. 모든 동적 값은 컴파일러가 관리하는 데이터 스택에 인라인으로 저장되며, 메모리는 스코프가 끝날 때 해제된다.
items.content_ko: Goose는 힙 할당기, 가비지 컬렉터, 수명 주석(lifetime annotation)이 없는 메모리 안전 시스템 프로그래밍 언어다. 이 저장소의 벤치마크에서는 C++와 Rust보다 빠르게 실행되면서도 메모리를 적게 쓴다고 한다. 문법은 C와 Rust 사용자에게 익숙하지만, 힙이 없다는 점이 가장 큰 차이다. 모든 동적 값은 컴파일러가 관리하는 데이터 스택에 인라인으로 놓인다. 스택은 포인터를 전진시키며 커지고, 메모리는 스코프가 끝나면 해제된다. 언어의 타입 및 수명 규칙이 이 메모리 모델을 안전하게 만든다. 프로그램은 네이티브 호출 스택, 정적 데이터, 그리고 N개의 데이터 스택을 가지며, N은 컴파일러가 결정한다. 각 데이터 스택은 bump pointer를 가진 큰 주소 공간 예약 영역이다. 스택마다 크기가 조정 가능한 값은 최대 하나만 살아 있으며, 항상 스택 맨 위에 있다. 따라서 증가할 때 아무것도 이동하지 않고 용량 검사도 필요 없다. 이 모든 것은 컴파일 시점에 증명되며, 런타임은 bump pointer만 관리한다.

items.title: I Bought a Custom Domain and So Should You
items.content:
Imagine you have been using the same email address for years. It is probably linked to all of your accounts, subscriptions, banking and pretty much everything else.

Now imagine your email provider shuts down, stops providing the service or you decide to leave because you're not happy with it. Changing your email address everywhere would be a nightmare.

This is where owning your custom domain comes in.

By owning a custom domain you can create an address like hello@yourdomain.com and use it with a compatible email service.

If you ever want to change providers you can update your domain’s email settings to point to the provider while keeping the same email address.

Your provider might change but your email address doesn't have to.

Email aliases let you use email addresses for different services without showing your main email address.

All these addresses can send emails to the same mailbox.

If one address starts getting spam you can turn it off without affecting the others. You can also reply to emails by copying a reverse-alias address (from SimpleLogin) from a specific alias you have created e.g. social@yourdomain.com and paste it in the recipient’s address so that when they receive the email the only address they will see is your chosen alias (e.g. social@yourdomain.com ).

I can use for example Proton Mail as my mailbox and SimpleLogin to handle my aliases.

Once I link SimpleLogin to my chosen mailbox and set up my custom domain I can create aliases from the SimpleLogin dashboard. Emails that arrive are sent to my Proton mailbox. I can send or reply through my aliases using the SimpleLogin reverse-alias feature.

For me the main advantage isn't just having unlimited aliases or keeping my main email address hidden. It is having control over my digital identity.

My domain is separate from my email provider, which means I have freedom if I ever want to switch services.

Of course I will have to keep my domain active, protect my registrar account, keep my DNS settings right and have an email service.

Overall I think the freedom is worth it.

If you have been using the same email address for years and want more control over your digital identity think about getting your own domain and pair it with an email service that supports custom domains. You can make switching providers much easier in the future.

It's a cost that can save you a lot of trouble later.

items.title: Fully customise your select elements
items.content:
For years and years, developers have had to come up with all sorts of creative workarounds to style <select> dropdown menus.

I covered this a good while ago in Form styling limitations are an accessibility issue , and I can’t tell you how excited I was when Safari 27 included ‘Customisable Select’, following Chrome’s lead from early last year.

Some years ago, there was a proposal for a new <selectmenu> HTML element . That would have meant replacing existing <select> s to take advantage of it, and working out what to show people whose browsers didn’t support the new element.

The approach we’ve ended up with builds on <select> instead, which makes things much simpler.

If you’re already using <select> and have styled it as far as browsers allowed, there’s just some CSS to rewrite. Now, browsers that support the new styling get your custom design; those that don’t show their default <select> . A bit ugly, perhaps, but entirely usable.

Of course, developers who’ve needed fully custom-styled selects have long reached for <div> s, <span> s, JavaScript, and ARIA instead. If that’s what you’re working with, there’s still some replacement work to do, just as there would have been with <selectmenu> . You’ll need to swap the hand-built component for a <select> , then add your styles.

Either way, we now have a native HTML element we can style properly, with a fallback built in.

For reference, this is the markup at its simplest:

< label for = " fruit " > What is your favourite fruit? </ label >

< select id = " fruit " name = " fruit " >

< option disabled selected > Choose one </ option >

First, we need to opt into the new base styling. This applies to both the <select> button and its dropdown menu, which is called the ‘picker’:

This gives us a more neutral starting point:

A downward-pointing chevron/arrow on the button

The picker positioned underneath the button

Some things look slightly different between browsers, but the good news is we can now override those styles easily.

This is super straightforward. Just use whatever styles you like, for example:

You can replace the chevron using the ::picker-icon pseudo-element:

And use the :open pseudo-class to change the icon when the picker is open:

And the picker is just as easy to style:

Now it matches its button! We can use margin-top to put a bit of distance between it and its trigger, add animations; whatever we like!

We can style the options using option {} , and target the checkmark with the ::checkmark pseudo-element:

Use :checked if you want to make the selected option stand out a bit more:

You can go further by adding images and other markup to your options, and use <selectedcontent> to display that richer content in the button too, but I’ll stick with plain old text for now.

The features we’ve used to customise our <select> s ( appearance: base-select , ::picker-icon , and ::picker(select) ) aren’t supported in Firefox yet, but work in Chrome and Chromium-based browsers like Edge and Opera, as well as Safari 27.

At the time of writing, that covers around 72% of global browser usage. Safari 27 is still new, so there’s plenty of room for that to grow as people update to the latest operating system; Apple appears to be rolling out iOS 27 more slowly than usual .

But we don’t need to wait for every browser to catch up. Those that don’t support the new styling show the unstyled <select> , so people can still choose an option and complete the form.

I don’t use <select> elements very much as <input type="radio" /> is usually a better alternative, but, where a <select> is needed, I’ll be using this new technique. It gives me control over the styling and falls back nicely if browser support isn’t there.

items.content_ko: 개발자들은 수년간 <select> 드롭다운을 꾸미기 위해 다양한 우회 방법을 써 왔다. 작성자는 Safari 27이 Chrome에 이어 'Customisable Select'를 지원하게 된 점을 반기고 있다. 과거에는 기존 <select>를 대체할 새 <selectmenu> 요소가 제안된 적이 있었지만, 이 방식은 기존 요소를 바꿔야 하고 미지원 브라우저의 표시 방식도 따로 고민해야 했다. 최종적으로 채택된 방식은 기존 <select>를 기반으로 하므로 훨씬 단순하다. 이미 <select>를 쓰고 있다면 CSS만 고치면 된다. 지원하는 브라우저는 커스텀 디자인을 보여주고, 지원하지 않는 브라우저는 기본 <select>를 보여준다. 완전히 커스텀한 select를 위해 <div>, <span>, JavaScript, ARIA를 써 온 경우에는 대체 작업이 여전히 필요하다. 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.content:

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-115627 📢 Source: EEF 💣 CVSS Score: 6 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash_postgres allows a user to load destination records linked to a source record only through another tenant's join rows. When a many_to_many relationship, or a through relationship, is loaded with a lateral join (for example with a per-record limit or sort), AshPostgres.DataLayer builds the query for the join resource, and for each resource along a through path, in lateral_join_query/3 and through_step_queries/4 without running that resource's read action, which is where attribute multitenancy is applied. When those resources use strategy :attribute multitenancy, rows belonging to other tenants were joined, so the load returned destination records that the caller's tenant is not related to. This issue affects ash_postgres: from 0.38.0 before 2.15.2. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-25T19:49:50.510Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115627

items.title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
items.content:
Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC.

I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view.

It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer.

The lesions come from MILK10k , a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology:

100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses.

100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses.

Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician.

Basal cell carcinoma on the trunk of a 75-year-old man. All three models answered correctly.

Invasive melanoma under 0.8 mm thick, with very little pigment. GPT-6 Astra called it a basal cell carcinoma with 95% confidence. Claude Fable 5.1 and the CNN called it a melanoma.

Seborrhoeic keratosis on the leg. Both LLMs called it an actinic keratosis and the CNN a squamous cell carcinoma: all three were wrong, though all three would have kept it rather than discharge it.

Figure 2. Three more of the 200 test lesions. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC.

The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case.

The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses.

You can try the CNN yourself . Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions.

Figure 3. Correct first-choice diagnosis for the two LLMs and the CNN, which chose from the same six diagnoses. Labels show correct answers out of the number of lesions with that histology.

items.title: Partial Order Precedence
items.content:
This page contains a curated list of recent changes to main branch Zig.

This page contains entries for the year 2026 . Other years are available in

As of yesterday, the second oldest open proposal for the Zig language was issue #114: require parentheses sometimes to disambiguate confusing operator precedence , opened February 8, 2016. Ten years later, that proposal has been implemented in the master branch version of Zig thanks to contributor CMDRZero .

This means that some combinations of operators no longer have a defined precedence, and for those that don’t, the compiler will now require parentheses:

However, common cases can remain parenthesis-free:

The idea behind this is to reduce the number of rules a programmer needs to know when reading and writing Zig code. For example, no matter how experienced you are with Zig, it’s unlikely that you’d be able to explain the evaluation order of the following expression without looking up the precedence rules:

Still quite hairy, and not something I’d like to see in the wild, but nonetheless it’s understandable without knowing any precedence rules beyond arithmetic and comparison. Outside of this contrived example, though, the expressions that will now require parentheses are relatively rare (353 lines needed changes out of the million+ lines of code in the Zig codebase).

In practice, going forward, you will only need to remember the rules around operator combinations that still have a defined/unambiguous precedence. For example, when reading or writing code involving arithmetic operators, you’ll only need to remember the following precedence table:

You might notice that there isn’t anything too surprising there, and that lack of surprise was a (subjective) guiding principle for what should and should not require parentheses. As an example, while % has unambiguous precedence with regards to addition/subtraction operators, parentheses must be used when mixing % with multiplication/division operators, and with itself. However, this, and other ambiguous operator combinations, aren’t something you’ll need to commit to memory. Any (future) code you read will already have parentheses to disambiguate, and for any code you write, the compiler will let you know when you need parentheses.

For the full explanation, and to see the relevant precedence tables pertaining to other operators, see the updated Precedence section of the language reference .

My personal recommendation would be option 1, as the process of redetermining the intended evaluation order for these uncommon precedence scenarios can occasionally serve to uncover bugs ( here’s an example of that ).

If you go with option 2, I’d still recommend perusing the diff afterwards to ensure that nothing looks unusual, or is different than you expected/intended. A potentially common example of that is something like a orelse b() catch c which previously evaluated to (a orelse b()) catch c , but changing that to a orelse (b() catch c) likely makes more sense, even if the end result is unaffected. Also worth noting that in some scenarios, redundant parentheses will be added by zig fmt --upgrade (e.g. you might see something like a orelse ((b + c) - d) where the parentheses around b + c are unnecessary), so avoiding that will take a bit of manual cleanup.

That’s about it. I’m hopeful that this change will make bugs stemming from misremembered precedence rules much less likely, and that it will put some attention onto any of those bugs that may currently exist.

Thanks again to CMDRZero for the implementation, and to Isaac Freund for help with the corresponding grammar changes.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: AI Billionaires Are Flooding Money Into Politics to Influence Elections, But It’s Backfiring: Even a whiff of AI money seems to disgust voters.
items.content:
Unreasonably wealthy AI plutocrats are pouring billions of dollars into US elections.

Elon Musk alone has pumped more than $445 million into Republican campaigns ahead of the midterms, after spending a near-equal sum to get president Donald Trump elected in the last election cycle. Leading The Future, a Super PAC backed by OpenAI and Palantir cofounders and prominent tech venture capitalists including Marc Andreessen, has amassed $140 million to dole out to pro-AI candidates.

But all that money doesn’t seem to be helping the AI industry’s interests, because its image is still in the toilet .

A new analysis from Guardrails Action, an AI accountability advocacy group, found that voters in key battleground states still harbor mostly negative feelings towards the AI industry, with the tech being such a toxic topic that it’s potentially driving voters to cross the aisle.

The survey, reported by Inc , questioned over 3,000 likely voters in Iowa, Michigan, and Ohio — states where close Senate races are unfolding — about their thoughts on AI.

AI, the results showed, is a political landmine, with even a whiff of Big Tech money being potentially disastrous for a candidate’s image.

Three quarters of the likely voters said that they would be less apt to vote for a candidate if they found out they had accepted a donation from an AI Super PAC .

Some felt even more strongly than that. A quarter said they would switch parties to vote for a candidate who took a strong stance against AI companies and data center construction.

“We found that the AI Super PACs were more toxic with voters than Wall Street, cryptocurrency or AIPAC,” Charles Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, a PAC that combats AI spending that the advocacy group is part of, told Inc . “The influence of AI money on elections and politics sits at this nexus of the anxieties that people are feeling about AI, and this increased disgust people have around corruption and special interest money and politics.”

Ironically, this seems to be because voters are convinced by some of the noise coming out of the industry itself. Many luminaries in the industry have pushed doomy narratives about their tech destroying civilization, wiping out jobs, and possibly being conscious — while companies including Anthropic and OpenAI warn about their AIs going on rogue hacking sprees .

items.title: .NET October 2026 Out-of-Band Security Updates
items.content:
Today, we are releasing out-of-band (OOB) security updates for .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10, along with .NET 11 Release Candidate 3. We recommend updating as soon as possible.

This out-of-band release addresses CVE-2026-111497 , a vulnerability in the Brotli decompression algorithm . It also includes a fix for CVE-2026-114148 (Linux .NET tarball ownership) in .NET 8, 9, 10, and 11.

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in .NET’s use of the Brotli decompression algorithm. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege.

Unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs could allow a local attacker to modify files and gain elevated privileges.

Applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression , HttpClient automatic response decompression , or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs. Request decompression and automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. .NET Framework is not affected.

For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source.

For vulnerability details and affected products, see the linked security advisories.

Additionally, we are re-releasing the advisories for CVE-2026-70197 (SocketAsyncEventArgs memory corruption) in .NET 8, 9, 10, and 11, and CVE-2026-102870 (Blazor WebAssembly debugger) in .NET 10 and 11 because the October 13, 2026 release did not fully address these issues. Today’s updates provide those fixes.

.NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

Update your applications and build environments

Framework-dependent applications: Install the updated runtime for the .NET version your application targets, then restart the application.

Self-contained applications: Rebuild and republish with the updated runtime. Installing a newer runtime on the host does not update the runtime bundled with your application.

Containers: Rebuild and redeploy using updated .NET container images .

Source-build consumers: Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix.

ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and .NET 9: Update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version. This applies even if you do not build .NET from source.

You can check the runtimes installed on a machine with:

For framework-dependent deployments, confirm that the appropriate updated runtime listed above is installed. Self-contained applications and container deployments must be checked separately because they carry their own runtime.

See the .NET deployment documentation for more information about framework-dependent and self-contained applications.

If you encounter a problem after updating, report it in the .NET release feedback issues .

items.content_ko: 오늘 .NET 8, .NET 9, .NET 10용 긴급(OOB) 보안 업데이트와 .NET 11 Release Candidate 3를 배포한다. 가능한 한 빨리 업데이트할 것을 권장한다. CVE-2026-111497은 .NET의 Brotli 압축 해제 알고리즘에 존재하는 버퍼 오버플로 취약점으로, 인증되지 않은 공격자가 프로세스 메모리를 읽거나 손상시킬 수 있으며 정보 노출, 서비스 거부, 권한 상승으로 이어질 수 있다. CVE-2026-114148은 영향받는 .NET tarball의 안전하지 않은 소유권 메타데이터 문제로, 로컬 공격자가 파일을 수정하고 권한을 상승시킬 수 있다. 이 문제는 .NET 8, 9, 10, 11에서 수정되었다. ASP.NET Core 요청 압축 해제, HttpClient 자동 응답 압축 해제, System.IO.Compression Brotli API를 통해 Brotli 압축 데이터를 처리하는 애플리케이션이 영향을 받을 수 있다. 요청 압축 해제와 자동 응답 압축 해제는 기본적으로 활성화되어 있지 않다. .NET Framework는 영향을 받지 않는다. .NET 10과 11의 CVE-2026-114148은 소스 빌드 tarball에만 영향을 준다. 원문이 중간에 끊겨 있어 .NET 8 등의 세부 내용은 확인되지 않는다.

items.title: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
items.content:
One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.

In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second.

We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.

Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.

It scores an impressive 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 88.8%) and 91.2% on BrowseComp (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 90.4%). These results demonstrate frontier-level coding and agentic capabilities, even outperforming leading proprietary models on some benchmarks. Read more about Kimi K3 here .

To calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer.

Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is:

Dividing that payload by 93 layers then gives:

Now that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type:

Therefore, with Kimi K3’s 69 linear layers and 24 dense layers , we get:

This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers.

Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop.

It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip.

This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next.

Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages.

For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token.

This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one?

No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time.

While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them.

Each stage can also process a micro-batch , a small group of requests, rather than a single request. So the number of requests in flight is roughly the number of stages times the micro-batch size.

To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27
items.content:
As one of the managers of the Digital Dissident Devroom , I invite you to be part of a conversation we cannot afford to ignore.

Around the world, people are being silenced, monitored, and denied access to information. Free software can help change that, but only if we build it together. We need tools people can trust and control to communicate safely, expose the truth, and resist censorship.

This devroom brings together developers, researchers, activists, and everyone committed to digital freedom. We want real solutions, honest lessons, and collaboration across projects, not product pitches.

If you believe technology should serve people, not control them, join us. Bring your ideas, experience, and questions. Let’s build the tools that help keep freedom alive.

Our focus complements other devrooms, including Decentralized Internet and Privacy, which explores the broader decentralized ecosystem. While they focus on technologies, we focus on the people under threat and the complete chain of tools that can protect them.

Go to FOSDEM’s official CFP portal from here and login or register.

Then fill in the form and select “Digital Dissident” as a track.

Please note that by doing this you also accept the FOSDEM Code of Conduct.

Define: Digital Dissident Developer Room

Privacy and anonymity tools each have a home at FOSDEM: the network, security, decentralised and messaging rooms, and various main-track and lightning talks. Someone living under an authoritarian regime (Russia, Iran, China, Belarus, Myanmar and others) never uses a single tool, though. Their day-to-day security depends on a chain of tools that has to hold up end to end:

reaching the network at all (censorship circumvention),

collecting, verifying and storing evidence safely,

publishing or leaking it without exposing the author,

doing all this on devices and infrastructure that are themselves a risk.

The weakest link decides the outcome. Talks about one tool rarely cover how it fits with the others, where the seams are, or what breaks at the hand-offs (for example, a circumvention transport that is fingerprinted, or a messenger whose push notifications tie your identity to a Google or Apple account). Nobody currently owns that cross-project view.

What this devroom does. It brings developers of circumvention, anonymity, messaging, publishing and whistleblowing tools into one room. It is deliberately not about any single project. Each session is judged on how well it advances the toolchain: interoperability, shared threat models, shared failure data, and shared engineering practice.

Why now. Censorship in Russia, Iran and China has grown much more sophisticated. It now includes national allow-lists and whitelist-only internet shutdowns, TLS and QUIC fingerprinting, deep packet inspection with active probing, throttling of specific protocols, mobile internet shutdowns, app-store removal of circumvention tools, and mandatory state-run messengers and “sovereign internet” routing. Anti-censorship developers have responded with pluggable transports, domain fronting alternatives, mixnets, decentralised and email-based messaging, and new obfuscation protocols. Progress is fast but fragmented. At FOSDEM 2026 the relevant talks were scattered: Vitaly Repin’s “The Russian Censorship Circumvention, Tom’s Traps, and Jerry’s VPN: A 5-Year Journey” (Saturday, H.1302, Network track) drew a large audience, while NymVPN and Delta Chat’s multi-relay messaging (both Sunday, Decentralized Internet and Privacy devroom) and other related talks ran in other rooms. A single devroom lets that audience and those speakers meet in one place.

Relationship to the existing “Decentralized Internet and Privacy” devroom. That room covers decentralised technology broadly (P2P protocols, browsers, code collaboration, key infrastructure), and censorship or anonymity is only a part of it. Digital Dissident is different: the organising principle is a user under threat and the end-to-end chain…

items.title: I want my Wednesday back
items.content:
Or, why we’re not seeing mass-exploitation of php2shell yet.

I saw wildly varying opinions on whether php2shell is serious, or if they cried wolf. Got curious, started digging into the PoCs. I’m not an exploit dev and maybe there were other factors, so take with a grain of salt. Egg on my face if mass exploitation starts right as I hit publish.

Best PoC of php2shell I’ve found: https://github.com/9bie/php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp (and a fork with all docs translated to english )

To exploit, you need to do four consecutive requests to the same php worker process . And you need to know the exact php build (php version, OS version, architecture), or try exploits for every possible build.

What this PoC does is take a docker image that uses the default mod_php number of workers, which is 150. Then it opens 149 connections that send half a request to keep the other workers busy, and does the four exploit requests against the 150th worker.

Even a moderately popular production website will have multiple web VMs/containers running multiple php workers behind a load balancer and constant bot traffic. That means you would have to try a wide range of number of connections to open. On top of that you likely won’t know the exact build version, so you would have to try exploits for every combination out there.

Let’s say you try this for the 50 most popular php/OS combinations, and any number of workers between 10 and 1010. That’s 50k attempts. But against constant background traffic, you would need to try each combination a number of times. Each of these attempts involves opening a whole lot of connections, so they each take some time. The PoC runs against localhost and takes 3-4 seconds, so let’s optimistically call it 10 seconds on the internet.

You can only do one attempt at a time, so that means multiple days of bruteforcing in a way that is essentially a DoS, since a large part of that range will exhaust the maximum number of connections. At this point the person running the site will likely notice, start blocking IP addresses or adding a WAF.

Most high-traffic websites already run WAFs/rate-limiting to deal with bot traffic, so you would need to run this attack from a great many IPs, and preferably clean ones that are harder to come by. But running this from many IPs also increases the chances that your timing will be off, reducing the number of plausible attempts even further.

That’s assuming the WAF doesn’t block your attempts entirely, because the easiest ways to exploit these vulnerabilities were known at the time of the announcement.

I’m sure people and agents will come up with clever techniques to reduce the required number of attempts eventually. But that has nothing to do with “this will get mass-exploited within 15 minutes.”

Against very low-traffic websites that do not have any bot protection, leak information about their version, running close to stock configuration, you might get lucky.

So sure, it’s a critical vulnerability, deserves attention, should be patched ASAP. Maybe even put in the announcement that if you’re running low-traffic sites, be extra sure to patch fast.

But to the AI security vendors who promoted this as THE GATES OF HELL WILL OPEN YOU HAVE TO PATCH WITHIN 15 MINUTES OR DIE? I want my Wednesday back.

Oh and the claims of it being exploited in the wild? At time of writing, they’re referring to exploitation attempts . In fact, HoneyLabs so far hasn’t seen a single exploit attempt that could even run successfully.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…
